scope: Actual DeepSeek V1,O1,C1 outputs after source caveats; comparisons are source-based, not template-similarity scoring.

cases.question: How would I work out what a company is worth before deciding whether its shares are a bargain?
cases.assessment: Useful intrinsic-value definition, cash-flow focus, uncertainty and per-share comparison. Not accepted as written: unsupported valuation rules and mathematical/generalization defects remain.

findings.answer_excerpt: many investors use “look-through earnings” or owner earnings as a rough proxy
findings.problem: A single audience member proposed look-through earnings as a proxy; the source does not establish this general practice or treat owner earnings and look-through earnings as equivalent.

findings.answer_excerpt: The rate should reflect the time value of money and the risk of the cash flows
findings.problem: Introduces a risk/required-return/opportunity-cost prescription unsupported by the selected originals. The separate 1998 packet rejects using a higher rate to compensate for not understanding the business; that context was not selected here.

findings.answer_excerpt: This means owner earnings are typically less than reported earnings
findings.problem: Capex exceeding depreciation does not establish c greater than the complete b. The 2004 Berkshire-specific capex expectation is also generalized to businesses.

findings.answer_excerpt: project distributable cash over a period (say, 20 years) and then estimate a terminal value
findings.problem: Turns an audience calculation into a prescribed step-by-step method. The reply accepts general cash valuation but questions variables; it does not validate a 20-year horizon or perpetual-coupon assumption.

cases.question: What makes reported profit different from cash an owner can actually take out of a business?
cases.assessment: Useful full owner-earnings formula and correct working-capital subtraction. Not accepted as written: later explanation still contradicts the full formula and misstates the EBITDA exception.

findings.problem: Narrows complete noncash component b to depreciation, then repeats this narrowed comparator for the oil-industry claim. Correct full formula elsewhere does not repair the contradiction.
Conflates EBITDA with reported earnings plus all specified noncash addbacks; then transfers the limited cash-flow shorthand exception to EBITDA under the same heading.

findings.answer_excerpt: A business that requires little or no capital to grow
findings.problem: The See’s example cited is maintenance expenditure exceeding depreciation by $500,000–$1m, not evidence of capital required for growth or of higher owner earnings relative to reported profit.

cases.question: How can I tell whether I really understand a business, rather than just know its products?
cases.assessment: Useful product/enterprise distinction and restored exact Berkshire-credit uncertainty. Not accepted as written: universalizes Berkshire preferences and adds a wrong-company attribution.

findings.answer_excerpt: simplicity and stability are prerequisites for understanding
findings.problem: Transforms Berkshire’s self-described limitations/preferences into a universal prerequisite. The final checklist similarly says the user cannot understand a changing business and must establish decades of competitive strength.

findings.answer_excerpt: Buffett uses Coca-Cola as an example
findings.problem: Combines the Coke passage with the adjacent See’s statement about purchase motivations unchanged since the 1920s, thereby assigning the latter claim to the wrong company.

findings.answer_excerpt: he did not regard the whole enterprise as within his circle of competence
findings.problem: The full quotation usefully restores uncertainty about Berkshire credit, but the following paraphrase again drops necessarily. Keep the qualified whole-enterprise judgment.

limits: Selected original paragraphs and speaker fields mechanically matched packet; this does not establish transcript/audio accuracy.
Source-specific notes do not guarantee obedience or semantic correctness.
No model ranking inferred from these three convenience-sample outputs.
